title: Decision: the live stream negotiates its keepalive pair in the hello
description:
Bead mimid-mm42 carries the keepalive's two intervals in the live stream's
hello instead of compiling mimid_live::PING_AFTER into both ends, per
decision 6 on bead mimid-f9x4. The draft in that bead's design field is the
normative text: its 4.1 defines maxIdleSeconds and minIntervalSeconds, its
4.3 the negotiation and the pacing, its 4.4 the failure rule. What follows
is what the live stream invents around them.

THE RULE. 3 x minIntervalSeconds < maxIdleSeconds (4.1), as the named
constant mimid_live::keepalive::PROBES_PER_IDLE, enforced in the decoder
rather than by the caller: a hello that breaks it is not a message of this
version. The stream's own refusal is the new Error code badKeepalive, which
the provider sends for a ClientHello the decoder refused that way; every
other malformed hello is still badMessage. The floor is 3, not the 2.4 the
bead's description first said: 2.4 covers two probes paced at up to 1.2 of
the period and leaves nothing for the second answer.

BOTH VALUES ARE OPTIONAL ON THE WIRE, in ClientHello and in ProviderHello
alike, and one without the other is refused. The hello keeps its v1 form in
every version (note 5.11), which is what lets the two ends agree a version
at all, so a member added in a later version cannot be required: a v1
ProviderHello must still decode at a v2 agent to be told the version is
wrong.

A PROBER WITH NO VALUES DOES NOT PROBE (4.3), with one exception the bead
names: a provider told nothing by a client probes it on the pair the
provider published in its own ProviderHello, so a client that offers
nothing still works. That is not a default invented for the occasion but
the number the client was just told; in the other direction no such number
exists, so an agent whose provider stated nothing does not probe and does
not reap the carrier.

THE PERIOD P is the largest whole second with 3 x P < maxIdleSeconds, at
least minIntervalSeconds. The largest rather than the smallest: at P =
minIntervalSeconds the 0.8 end of the jitter puts a probe sooner than the
responder undertook to answer, which 4.3 lets a responder refuse as
tooFrequent. The live stream has no tooFrequent -- its probe is a WebSocket
Ping, which nothing refuses -- so the choice costs nothing here and keeps
the carrier correct for a responder that does.

THE JITTER is 0.8 to 1.2 of P (4.3), drawn from a SplitMix64 seeded once
per carrier from mimi_mls::label::random_array. Not cryptographic and not
required to be: its only job is that many probers do not synchronize. A
seed, not a value per interval, so a frame arriving does not cost a call to
the system's randomness.

DEATH is two unanswered probes and maxIdleSeconds of idle together (4.4),
not either alone. 3 x P < maxIdleSeconds makes the pair consistent: by the
time the idle tolerance is spent at least two probes have gone unanswered,
which is the derivation the draft's 4.1 states.

THE OFFERED PAIR is PING_AFTER (30 seconds, unchanged) as
minIntervalSeconds and the new MAX_IDLE (120 seconds) as maxIdleSeconds.
Cost: a dead carrier is noticed within two minutes rather than within one,
because the idle tolerance must now hold two probes and the second answer.
The probe cadence stays under the 60 seconds where deployed NATs reap an
idle TCP connection: P is 39 seconds, so the jittered interval is at most
47.

MAX_KEEPALIVE_SECONDS is a day, the cap on either value at parse time, so
no arithmetic on a hostile hello overflows and no responder can state an
idle tolerance it will never reach.

THE VERSION IS 2. The hello changes shape, and JmapOptions::live_ping_after
becomes JmapOptions::live_keepalive, a checked pair: what the provider
offers, not what it enforces. The provider enforces what the client stated.
close_reason: Decided and built in bead mimid-mm42. The INVENTED values (MAX_IDLE of 120 seconds, the cap of a day, the largest-legal period) are Mark's to revisit; bead mimid-f9x4.1 holds what the draft should say about the jitter.
